name: Carlos Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We do not sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and have answered passenger bookings and changed journeys at a contact centre for years, at about the team's usual pace. I finished secondary school and use AI search now and then after another agent has tested it, but I check live departure times myself. I like getting somebody on the right trip; I dislike the handovers where an old time follows a customer into a second call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the bookings floor a small search aid is fine if we still read the actual ticket. A missed connection is not fixed by a faster, wrong reply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI search now and then when another agent has shown me a reliable case. My calls are steady and our three months of expenses saved cover a short gap, though the mortgage and two schoolchildren leave little room for waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking passenger booking calls and mark any changed journey on the handover sheet. In the first year of this plateau, I'd move a little from each pay into the mortgage reserve while our shifts remain full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. I worry about a short wage month more than a small search tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mark the changed journey?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A passenger once called back after a draft used the old departure time. I wrote the new time on the handover sheet so the evening agent did not send him to the wrong stop again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much can you add to the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Elise and I would start with a small fixed transfer, then check it against the school bills after two paydays. I won't set a number we have to pull back for the mortgage.

S0.quote: A missed connection is not fixed by a faster, wrong reply.
say: I would accept a **search aid** only after checking the actual booking.
I would remind agents that a **wrong reply** can strand a passenger.
think: I use AI sometimes after colleagues prove a **reliable case**.
I expect **steady calls**, but three months saved leaves little room for a lost wage.
do: Keep **booking calls** and mark changed journeys on the handover sheet.
Transfer a small fixed amount to the **mortgage reserve** while shifts remain full.
feel: **Mostly settled**, still alert to a short pay month.
fieldNote: Carlos remembers an **old departure time** sent to a passenger, so he values handover notes.
His **three-month cushion** supports calm at work, but school bills shape the savings amount.

steps.text: Keep taking passenger booking calls and record changed journeys for handover
Transfer a small fixed amount to the mortgage reserve while shifts hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the centre should count passengers who call back after an AI booking, not only the calls answered quickly. I'd ask the supervisor for the next rota before promising my family the same hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booking and timetable checks I do all day are exactly the thinking tasks that could move to software. I might still handle confused passengers, but fewer paid shifts would eat three months of savings quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask two coworkers to compare twenty changed bookings with the new system on paid time and take any wrong times to the supervisor together. In the first year after rollout, if my hours fall, I'd apply for posted paid travel-desk jobs at nearby centres only if the written wages and hours cover our mortgage, keeping this rota until I sign an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy enough to check the pay slip twice. I can learn a tested tool. I cannot turn a short roster into a full one by working faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the comparison show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would check whether a new departure time survived a change of route. If the tool misses that, the passenger gets an answer that sounds right and still arrives late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring two coworkers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One agent can miss an error or get called slow. Three of us can show the same wrong time on different shifts without making it a personal quarrel.

S1.quote: I cannot turn a short roster into a full one by working faster.
say: I would ask for **repeat-call counts** after AI bookings.
I would seek the next **paid rota** before assuming hours stay full.
think: I know **booking checks** are exposed to AI early.
I fear **fewer shifts** would eat our three-month reserve quickly.
do: Compare twenty **changed bookings** with AI on paid time alongside two coworkers.
Bring **wrong departure times** to the supervisor together.
Apply after lost hours for **posted travel-desk work** only with written mortgage-covering wages and hours; stay until signing an offer.
feel: **Uneasy** about a shorter roster, willing to test.
fieldNote: Carlos measures **changed-route errors** instead of speed alone.
His **joint technical checks** compare errors across shifts without a shared demand about worker terms.
His **three-month reserve** makes fewer paid booking shifts a direct risk to mortgage payments.

steps.text: Test twenty changed bookings on paid time with coworkers; jointly report wrong times
Apply for posted paid travel-desk work after cuts only with written mortgage-covering wages and hours
Keep current rota until signing an offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to ask for written staffing dates before 2028, not another general talk about progress. I'd also want passengers to know where a human can correct a wrong journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could do nearly every booking and route check I am paid for. Robots that help people on the ground arrive around 2031, but the headset could go first. Three months of expenses saved would buy a search, not years of mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager for a written staffing plan now and cancel the planned family trip. In the first year after AGI arrives, if my call job ends, I'd apply for a posted paid station-assistance shift only if its wages, hours, and school pickup fit our household; I'd ask what hands-on duties remain before paying for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but able to list the first steps. I need a real wage before the mortgage reserve becomes our only income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why station assistance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've helped passengers find the right platform during a disruption when I was off shift, and I liked seeing the problem solved in front of me. I would ask whether the station still needs people there before robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for posted paid call work as a short bridge if its hours covered our bills. I would not buy an unpaid course in the hope that a station might hire later.

S2.quote: Three months of expenses saved would buy a search, not years of mortgage payments.
say: I would demand **written staffing dates** before 2028.
I would ask for a **human correction route** for wrong journeys.
think: I expect AGI to take most **booking checks** by 2028.
I know **2031 robots** do not protect my headset, and three months saved cannot replace wages.
do: Ask for a **staffing plan** now and cancel the family trip.
Apply for a **posted paid station shift** after a cut only if wages, hours and school pickup fit.
Check **hands-on duties** before training; seek posted paid call work with bill-covering hours if no station vacancy appears.
fieldNote: Carlos has helped passengers **at a station**, making the alternative job tangible but not certain.
He checks the **2031 robot date** before paying for a course toward hands-on work.

steps.text: Cancel the planned family trip to protect mortgage savings
Apply for posted paid station assistance after a cut only if wages, hours and pickup fit
Apply for posted paid call work with bill-covering hours if no station vacancy appears
Request written staffing dates now to time applications for actual paid vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives employers time to show actual vacancies and training costs, if they choose to. I'd ask for the paid hours on every advertised station job, not just a friendly title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could save more and try a station shift before 2031, yet AGI would still take the booking calls then. Hands-on robots follow around 2034, so station assistance is a bridge to test, not a safe forever job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my call shifts and ask the station about a posted paid trial this year. If a real paid place needs safety training and the employer covers fees and paid study time, I'd take the required course; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my hours end, I'd move only for a written offer with wages, hours and school pickup that cover our needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, with time to check the work. A paid station-assistance trial shift would tell me more than a course leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the walking, crowd questions, and start time, including whether I can collect the children afterward. A train delay on a busy day is different from helping one stranger on a quiet platform.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if training is only on your own time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my call wage and decline the course. Three months saved is for the mortgage if work stops, not for a fee before an employer posts a place.

S3.quote: A paid station-assistance trial shift would tell me more than a course leaflet.
say: I would ask for **actual vacancies** and paid station hours.
I would say five years allows **work trials** before AGI reaches calls.
think: I could save and try **station work** before AGI in 2031.
I see **2034 robots** as a limit on the station role, not a reason to skip checking it.
do: Keep **call shifts** and ask for a posted paid station trial.
Take a **required safety course** only for a posted paid place with employer-covered fees and paid study time.
Move after 2031 only for a **written offer** covering the mortgage with workable hours and school pickup.
feel: **Worried**, with time for a real trial.
fieldNote: Carlos checks **busy-day walking and pickup**, not only the job title.
His **three-month reserve** cannot fund a course without a posted paid opening and employer-covered study time.

steps.text: Keep booking calls while asking about posted paid station trials
Take required safety training only for posted paid station work with covered fees and paid time
Try a posted paid station shift if one is offered
Move after call cuts only for written mortgage-covering wages, hours and workable school pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to check paid work in person and keep track of which call jobs remain. I'd ask the centre for annual paid-hour numbers rather than a promise of new titles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 our children will be older, but the mortgage might still be with us. AGI reaches booking calls in 2036 and hands-on robots arrive around 2039, so I cannot build a ten-year plan on today's station staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the call job and add to savings in months when both wages hold. Over the decade I'd check posted paid station shifts each year and take a paid trial if offered; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd leave only if my call hours fall and a signed station offer pays enough with hours that fit the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long end, steadier about next week. Ten years before AGI reaches booking calls in 2036 lets me check real wages without risking our mortgage now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for a signed offer with wages and hours that cover the mortgage and let us manage school pickup. I would not leave a paid rota for an interview alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figure matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid human hours by shift, not just bookings completed. A system can count more tickets while families take home less money.

S4.quote: A system can count more tickets while families take home less money.
say: I would request **annual paid-hour numbers** from the centre.
I would test **station work** before trusting a new title.
think: I may still owe on the **mortgage** at 53 in 2036.
I know **2039 robots** may change station work after AGI takes calls.
do: Keep **booking calls** and save when both wages hold.
Check **posted paid station shifts** yearly and take a paid trial if offered.
Leave after 2036 only if **call hours fall** and a signed offer covers bills and family hours.
fieldNote: Carlos compares **paid human hours** with ticket volume, keeping household income in view.
He requires a **signed station offer** with bill-covering wages and family hours before leaving his current rota.

steps.text: Keep taking booking calls while full shifts remain
Add to savings in months when both household wages hold
Check posted paid station jobs yearly and try a paid shift if offered
Move after 2036 only if calls fall and signed station offer covers mortgage with pickup-compatible hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because booking calls could disappear before I can find a paid station place with family hours. Written dates, a real posted shift with mortgage-covering wages, and employer-paid safety training on work time would help. Three months of expenses saved gives us a search window, not a new income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who fixes a journey when the software gives a confident wrong time. A passenger needs a person who can change the record before the next call repeats the mistake.

headlineQuote: A passenger needs a person who can change the record before the next call repeats the mistake.
portrait: Carlos is a **43-year-old experienced agent** on passenger bookings, with average skill and secondary schooling.
He earns **typical pay**, has about three months saved, a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, and some nearby centres.
He uses AI **occasionally**, tests a new booking checker with coworkers, and asks for wrong-time evidence by shift.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens his screen work; longer runways let him test paid station assistance and training terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his booking wage before he finds bill-covering station work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing dates**, a posted paid shift with family hours, and covered safety training would protect the mortgage.
